title: Chapter XLII

teacherSummary.text: Elizabeth reflects on her parents' poorly matched marriage. She tours with the Gardiners to Derbyshire, near Pemberley, Darcy's estate.

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “Chapter XLII,” how does Austen show an unhappy marriage observed? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the characterization you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: High School / Common Core
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter XLII develops the idea of an unhappy marriage observed. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of characterization and theme shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Jane Austen uses characterization in Chapter XLII to complicate the reader's understanding of an unhappy marriage observed. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter XLII within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of an unhappy marriage observed responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter XLII as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of an unhappy marriage observed. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Pride and Prejudice.

satQuestions.passage: Elizabeth, however, had never been blind to the impropriety of her father’s behaviour as a husband. She had always seen it with pain; but respecting his abilities, and grateful for his affectionate treatment of herself, she endeavoured to forget what she could not overlook, and to banish from her thoughts that continual breach of conjugal obligation and decorum which, in exposing his wife to the contempt of her own children, was so highly reprehensible. But she had never felt so strongly as now the disadvantages which must attend the children of so unsuitable a marriage, nor ever been so fully aware of the evils arising from so ill-judged a direction of talents; talents which rightly used, might at least have preserved the respectability of his daughters, even if incapable of enlarging the mind of his wife.
satQuestions.prompt: Which choice best states a central concern of “Chapter XLII”?

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: What has Elizabeth learned from her parents' marriage? No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script: Today's words are curtailed, enhance, acquiesce, captivated, conjugal. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check Webster's. Here is the first: “Gardiner, which at once delayed its commencement and curtailed its extent.” Webster's says: To cut off the end or tail, or any part, of. Now the word history: “curtail”: cur (Latin cura, "care"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary. “enhance”: en- (French en-/Latin in-, "into"). Root not in our table: have students find it. “acquiesce”: ac- (Latin ad, "to"). Root not in our table: have students find it. Add each root to your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of Pride and Prejudice would have known. Country house tourism was common; housekeepers guided visitors when owners were away. Why does this chapter matter? The parents' marriage illustrates the cost of choosing on looks alone. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for characterization.
segments.script: Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. I read a sentence, stop, and ask what the author is doing. When I see characterization, I underline it and write in the margin what effect it has. Here I notice the diction and the sentence rhythm, and I connect them to an unhappy marriage observed.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Characterization, Theme, Setting.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of characterization. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.
segments.passage: Elizabeth, however, had never been blind to the impropriety of her father’s behaviour as a husband. She had always seen it with pain; but respecting his abilities, and grateful for his affectionate treatment of herself, she endeavoured to forget what she could not overlook, and to banish from her thoughts that continual breach of conjugal obligation and decorum which, in exposing his wife to the contempt of her own children, was so highly reprehensible. But she had never felt so strongly as now the disadvantages which must attend the children of so unsuitable a marriage, nor ever been so fully aware of the evils arising from so ill-judged a direction of talents; talents which rightly used, might at least have preserved the respectability of his daughters, even if incapable of enlarging the mind of his wife.

Then open your writing prompt; your level is already set. Middle-school version: In “Chapter XLII,” how does Austen show an unhappy marriage observed? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the characterization you noticed as one piece of evidence. I will circulate and conference.

segments.activity: Structured discussion (think-pair-share or a short Socratic circle).
segments.script: Let's talk. Our question: How does this chapter connect to first impressions and prejudice? Every claim needs a page reference. Respond to the person before you by agreeing, extending or challenging with evidence.

segments.activity: Chapter quiz in the app, then a one-sentence exit ticket.
segments.script: Take the chapter quiz in the app. Then, in one sentence, tell me what this chapter suggests about an unhappy marriage observed, backed by one short quotation.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
